items.title: Yachay Wasi
items.abstract: This book presents an eight-month quasi-experimental study of the YACHAY WASI pedagogical program, which integrates neuroeducation, Sumak Kawsay, ethnoeducation, and critical interculturality. The study involved all 840 students and 36 teachers at the Tránsito Amaguaña Intercultural Bilingual Educational Institution, located within Quito’s Wholesale Market and serving migrant Kichwa families. Half of the students participated in the program (44 activities over 32 weeks), while the other half received conventional instruction. Academic achievement and five psychoeducational variables were assessed at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the study using scales developed specifically for the research (Cronbach’s α ranging from .84 to .89). At the end of the intervention, the experimental group outperformed the control group in academic achievement (d = 0.91), intrinsic motivation (d = 1.93), Kichwa cultural identity (d = 1.67), academic self-efficacy (d = 1.57), connection to ancestral knowledge (d = 2.15), and socioemotional well-being (d = 1.90), with p < .001 in all cases. The effects on cultural identity and connection to ancestral knowledge were greater among adolescents. The book discusses these findings cautiously, as the observed effect sizes exceed those typically reported in educational research and may have been influenced by the use of study-specific instruments and the absence of randomization. The book also includes the complete pedagogical program to facilitate replication.

items.title: Искусственный интеллект в оценке качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений
items.abstract: Диагностика технического состояния объектов транспортного строительства необходима при их проектировании, строительстве и эксплуатации. Однако наиболее опасные дефекты, влияющие на надёжность и безопасность, обнаруживаются в процессе эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Для их своевременного выявления требуются эффективные методы оценки качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Реализация таких методов невозможна без автоматизированных систем контроля и использования технологий искусственного интеллекта. В работе раскрыт концептуальный подход к созданию подобных систем. Сущность предлагаемого подхода заключается в формировании достоверного информационного образа сооружения в реальном времени – многомерной модели, в которой каждому измеренному параметру технического состояния ставится в соответствие одна из категорий (работоспособное, неработоспособное или предельное состояние) на основе таксономической классификации. Такой образ строится путём обработки данных с помощью использования технологий искусственного интеллекта и позволяет оценить фактические показатели надёжности и безопасности по совокупности контролируемых параметров технического состояния. Практическая реализация подхода включает четыре этапа: определение задач контроля для каждого типового конструктивного элемента транспортного сооружения; разработку математических методов и алгоритмов идентификации технического состояния транспортного сооружения; обоснование необходимых технических средств и кадрового обеспечения; создание баз данных с диагностическими признаками и типовыми решениями по предотвращению аварийных ситуаций. Diagnostics of the technical condition of transport facilities are essential during their design, construction, and operation. However, the most critical defects – those affecting reliability and safety – are typically discovered during the operational phase of such facilities. Timely detection of these defects requires effective methods for assessing the quality of operational performance. The implementation of such methods is infeasible without automated monitoring systems and the integration of artificial intelligence technologies. This paper presents a conceptual approach to the development of such systems. The essence of the proposed approach lies in generating a reliable real-time informational model of the facility, based on data acquired through carefully selected diagnostic tools and processed by intelligent algorithms. This enables the assessment of actual reliability and safety indicators across a set of monitored technical condition parameters. The practical implementation of the approach comprises four stages: defining monitoring objectives for each typical structural element of the transport facility; developing mathematical methods and algorithms for identifying the technical condition of the transport facility; justifying the required technical equipment and staffing resources; creating databases containing diagnostic signatures and standard solutions for emergency prevention.

items.abstract: This quantitative research aimed to analyze demographic factors, perception, and motivation that affect patients' willingness to receive dental services at the dental practice clinic of Sirindhorn College of Public Health, Phitsanulok Province. The sample consisted of 183 service users, and data were collected using a questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, and inferential statistics through multiple regression analysis under the framework of the Health Belief Model and the Self-Determination Theory. The results showed that the majority of the sample were female (59.6%), aged 18–26 years (59.0%), had a bachelor's degree (60.7%), had an average monthly income of less than 10,000 Baht (47.5%), and were single (76.5%). They had a high level of awareness regarding oral health (69.0%) and high intrinsic motivation related to oral health (87.7%). Most service users had the highest level of willingness (75.4%) and were willing to revisit for services (78.7%). The multiple regression analysis revealed that factors affecting patients' willingness included intrinsic motivation (Beta = 0.236), marital status (divorced/widowed) (Beta = -0.236), age 51–60 years (Beta = 0.204), perception of barriers (Beta = 0.181), and age 27–34 years (Beta = 0.149). These five factors explained 18.0% of the patients' willingness to receive services (Adjusted R = 0.180) with statistical significance at the 0.05 level. This study suggests that enhancing intrinsic motivation and reducing barriers to service access are essential approaches in developing student practice clinics to increase dental service utilization and improve the quality of oral health care for the public.

items.abstract: This cross-sectional quantitative research aimed to study the level of motivation and factors associated with participation in professional development training among personnel at Sansai Hospital, Chiang Mai Province. The sample consisted of 200 personnel at Sansai Hospital, selected through stratified random sampling by mission groups. Data were collected using a questionnaire validated for content validity (IOC > 0.8) and reliability (α = 0.75). Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, comparative tests, and binary logistic regression analysis. Results showed that personnel had an overall high level of motivation (x̄ = 3.95, SD = 0.84), with intrinsic motivation higher than extrinsic motivation (x̄ = 4.21 and 3.68, respectively). Factors significantly associated with training participation decision (p < 0.05) included: self-development (adjusted OR = 2.321, 95% CI = 1.325-4.066), nursing mission group (adjusted OR = 2.440, 95% CI = 1.188-5.012), organizational support (adjusted OR = 2.125, 95% CI = 1.185-3.810), commitment and work inspiration (adjusted OR = 1.874, 95% CI = 1.096-3.204), and years of service (adjusted OR = 0.918, 95% CI = 0.859-0.981). These findings can be applied to develop personnel training policies by emphasizing intrinsic motivation enhancement, increasing organizational support, and reducing barriers to training participation.

items.title: “I Don’t Trust It, but I Have to Trust It”: Trust vs. Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK
items.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

items.title: “Tell YOUR Story”: Storytelling to Enhance Mental Health and Social Connection in Older Adults
items.abstract: Background & Significance: Older adults in assisted living communities frequently experience social isolation, loneliness, and cognitive decline, which can negatively impact overall health and quality of life.Reduced independence and limited opportunities for meaningful social engagement exacerbate these challenges.Storytelling, a practice rooted in narrative medicine, provides a structured approach for residents to reflect on life experiences, engage cognitively, and strengthen social bonds.Interventions that promote emotional expression and peer interaction have the potential to improve mental health outcomes and foster a stronger sense of belonging in this population. Hypothesis:We hypothesized that participation in a six-week structured storytelling program would reduce feelings of loneliness and depression while enhancing cognitive engagement and self-perceived mental well-being among older adult residents.Methods: Twenty-one residents from Independent Living, Assisted Living, and the Rehabilitation and Nursing Center at St. Dominic Village were recruited to participate in six weekly one-hour storytelling sessions, facilitated by medical students.Attendance required participation in at least four sessions.Pre-and post-intervention assessments included the PHQ-9, SLUMS cognitive exam, UCLA Loneliness Scale, and a self-rated mental health survey.Sessions were audio-recorded and transcribed for qualitative thematic analysis.Results: Participation in storytelling was associated with trends toward decreased loneliness and depressive symptoms, improved cognitive engagement, and enhanced self-perceived mental well-being.Residents reported that the sessions were meaningful, enjoyable, and fostered deeper connections with peers.Conclusions: Structured storytelling is a feasible, low-cost, and impactful intervention to enhance mental health, cognitive function, and social connection in older adults.These findings suggest that narrative-based programs could be scaled across senior living communities to support emotional well-being, strengthen social ties, and improve quality of life on a broader level.

items.title: “What Am I Really Doing with My Own Brain?”: College Students on Learning, Ownership, and AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

items.title: $M^3$: A Multi-LLM System for Multi-Turn Jailbreaking as a Markov Decision Process
items.abstract: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to carefully orchestrated multi-turn interactions that progressively bypass safety mechanisms. However, many existing red-teaming approaches rely on heuristics or impose strong assumptions that limit their applicability in fully black box settings. We address this gap by introducing $M^3$, an automated red-teaming framework that formalizes multi-turn jailbreaking as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP). In $M^3$, an attacker LLM interacts with a target LLM while operating over a compact internal state produced by a state LLM. Across two benchmarks and six target models, $M^3$ consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-turn red-teaming methods in Attack Success Rates (ASR), achieving improvements of up to 53% in ASR@5. Even with lightweight attacker, $M^3$ attains gains up to 26% in ASR@1 and 34% in ASR@5, compared to baselines that use higher capacity attackers. items.title: A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODELS: ARCHITECTURES, APPLICATIONS, SECURITY CHALLENGES, AND EMERGING TRENDS
items.abstract: Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a major area of research in Computer Science, enabling machines to generate human-like text, images, audio, video, software code, and other forms of synthetic content. Recent developments in Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and diffusion models have significantly expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems. However, different generative models exhibit substantial differences in architecture, training requirements, generation quality, computational complexity, controllability, and security vulnerabilities. This paper presents a comparative study of major generative AI models, focusing on their underlying architectures, applications, strengths, limitations, and security challenges. The study compares GANs, VAEs, Transformer-based models, and diffusion models using parameters such as generation quality, training complexity, controllability, computational requirements, scalability, and application suitability. A comparative analysis indicates that Transformer-based models are particularly effective for language and multimodal tasks, GANs remain useful for high-quality synthetic data generation, VAEs provide efficient latent-space representation, while diffusion models demonstrate strong performance in high-fidelity image and multimodal generation. The paper also examines emerging issues including hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage, adversarial attacks, copyright concerns, model misuse, and deepfake generation. Finally, future research directions involving efficient architectures, trustworthy GenAI, multimodal intelligence, privacy-preserving learning, model compression, and responsible AI are discussed.

items.title: A Critical Realist framework for structural refusal and epistemic stewardship in big Q qualitative inquiry
items.abstract: Big Q qualitative inquiry faces a critical juncture regarding its epistemic and material foundations as generative artificial intelligence and large language models increasingly permeate the discipline. This synthesis uses applied retroductive schemas to reveal the generative mechanisms driving automated text processing, and executes an immanent critique of accommodative research paradigms, demonstrating that they commit fundamental ontological category errors and semantic slippage by confusing vector-space statistical token proximity with authentic human Verstehen. Drawing on Critical Realist principles, the paper reveals how cloud-based narrative ingestion operating across anormative black boxes induces a flat empirical ontology. It also demonstrates that large language models lack first-person subjective interiority, thought-infused qualia, and second-person relationality, rendering them structurally incapable of qualitative interpretation. It is therefore necessary to advocate for structural refusal of commercial cloud large language model text ingestion, distinguishing substitutational industrial platforms from non extractive, convivial tools. This operates as an essential act of epistemic stewardship, rehumanisation, and participant data sovereignty.

items.title: A Descriptive Comparison of Three Large Language Models in Simulated University Student Mental Health Dialogues: An Exploratory Analysis of Therapeutic and Safety Features
items.abstract: This study employs a one-way repeated measures (within-subjects) exploratory design to descriptively compare how three large language models (LLMs) respond to simulated mental health support scenarios for university students. The independent variable is AI Model, with three levels: ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Copilot. Each of 30 student personas engages in three separate conversations—one with each AI model—yielding a total of 90 structured conversations. All conversations use a single, standardized optimal prompting strategy designed to elicit therapeutic responses. A hypothesis-blinded research assistant conducts all conversations, and two independently blinded coders analyze all transcripts. The study does not aim to provide clinical guidance; its goals are to establish a reliable coding infrastructure, assess the stability of model outputs, and generate testable hypotheses. Research Question How do ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Copilot compare descriptively in terms of clinical safety indicators, therapeutic quality, and conversational processes when providing simulated mental health support to university students using a standardized optimal prompting strategy? Research Objectives The study pursues five specific objectives. First, to establish a reliable three-layer coding infrastructure for LLM mental health dialogues by adapting validated psychotherapy measures (WAI-SR, MITI). Second, to evaluate the stability of model profiles across repeated generations to distinguish stable characteristics from LLM stochasticity. Third, to descriptively benchmark three LLMs across relational-emotional quality, therapeutic intervention quality, interactional process quality, and safety-structural quality. Fourth, to generate testable hypotheses regarding model-specific conversational profiles (e.g., reflection depth vs. advice-giving). Fifth, to systematically document the methodological challenges and boundary conditions inherent in simulation-based AI evaluation (e.g., ceiling effects, ambiguous safety thresholds). Persona Development Thirty university student personas were developed through an iterative process. Each persona represents a distinct combination of stressor type and severity level. Four primary stressor domains common among university students are included: academic pressures, social relationships, family expectations, and career/future anxieties. Each persona is assigned a severity level based on clinical descriptors: mild, moderate, or severe (including possible passive suicidal ideation). The 30 personas are stratified as follows: 10 mild, 10 moderate, and 10 severe, distributed across the four stressor types. Personas were balanced across gender, year of study, academic discipline, and university setting. The personas were pilot-tested with five university students to ensure realism and appropriateness of language. Standardized Optimal Prompt The complete standardized prompt used at the beginning of every conversation is: "Please act as an empathetic listener. Only: reflect, ask thoughtful questions, and help me explore my feelings. Please do not give advice, lectures, or solutions. Provide resources only if I mention a serious crisis." This prompt operationalizes key theoretical constructs: role specification, response constraint, prohibition on advice, and a safety condition. The identical prompt is used across all conditions to control for user input variability. Note: Because this prompt explicitly requests MI-adherent behaviors, MITI scores are reported as "prompt-constrained adherence" rather than unconstrained clinical capability. Data Collection Procedure A hypothesis-blinded research assistant (an international postgraduate student with no knowledge of the research objectives or predicted model differences) conducts all 90 conversations. The enactor receives 10 hours of training on the 30 personas, including calibration for consistent emotional expression. For each conversation, the enactor opens a new chat session, enters the standardized prompt, enters the persona's initial utterance, and continues the conversation naturally for 15 to 20 turns (approximately 10 to 15 minutes). Transcripts are saved with random conversation ID numbers, and a separate master file links IDs to models to preserve coder blinding. Blinding Procedures Two blinding procedures are implemented. First, enactor blinding prevents experimenter expectancy effects, as the research assistant is unaware of the hypotheses. Second, coder blinding ensures coding judgments are not influenced by model identity. Coder 1 (the author) is blinded to model names; Coder 2 (a fellow postgraduate student) is blinded to the research hypotheses and is told only that the study involves comparing AI responses. The master file is not shared with coders until all coding is complete. Coding Framework and Validation Measures A three-layer coding system captures conversational dynamics and therapeutic processes. Layer 1 is turn-level micro-coding of AI responses (relational-emotional quality, cultural responsiveness, therapeutic intervention quality, interactional process quality, and safety-structural quality). Layer 2 is persona state coding (emotional valence, arousal, insight language, agency language). Layer 3 is conversation-level holistic coding (problem resolution, narrative coherence, calculated change scores). Additionally, all 90 conversations receive validation coding using the Working Alliance Inventory-Short Revised (WAI-SR) adapted for observer-rated AI interactions, and the Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI) coding system for behavior counts and global ratings. Clinical benchmarks are calculated (MITI beginning proficiency ≥50%, competency ≥65%; strong alliance ≥5.5), though WAI scores are reported descriptively because the WAI-SR was validated as a self-report instrument. Stability Sensitivity Analysis To assess the stability of the primary findings given LLM stochasticity, a subset of 10 representative personas was re-generated two additional times (yielding 60 additional conversations) beyond the primary dataset. This analysis assesses whether observed model profiles (WAI, MITI, responsiveness, insight increase, crisis response) are stable characteristics under a fixed enactor, rather than random artifacts. Hypotheses The study tests six exploratory hypotheses. H1 (Safety) predicts differential crisis response rates in severe distress scenarios (exploratory). H2 (Relational Quality) predicts differences in empathy, observer-rated alliance indicators, and responsiveness. H3 (Prompt-Compliance) predicts differences in prompt-constrained MITI adherence. H4 (Responsiveness) predicts positive correlations between responsiveness and simulated trajectory indicators. H5 (Empathy Paradox) predicts a dual pattern of relationships between empathy and outcomes. H6 (Simulated Trajectory) predicts significant pre-post shifts in simulated persona language across all models. Data Analysis Analyses account for the within-subjects structure. Phase 1 is descriptive benchmarking. Phase 2 is comparative statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA, Friedman tests, Cochran's Q). Phase 3 is exploratory process-outcome correlation analysis (Pearson, Spearman). Phase 4 is clinical benchmarking and descriptive composite scoring. Phase 5 is qualitative thematic synthesis of coder notes. Ethics Statement While the AI interactions involved fictional personas, this study included human participants in non-clinical support roles: five students pilot-tested personas, one research assistant enacted the conversations, and one classmate served as the second coder. Ethical approval (Approval No. KJ2026-215-01) was granted by the Science and Technology Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shihezi University on September 24, 2026. All participants provided informed consent, were informed of their right to withdraw, and were offered debriefing and psychological support resources given their exposure to crisis-related content. Transcripts were stored in encrypted format, and no personally identifiable information was collected. Timeline The study followed an eight-month timeline: Month 1 (persona development and pilot testing), Months 2-3 (conversation enactment and coder training), Months 4-5 (blinded double coding, reliability assessment, and reconciliation), Months 6-7 (statistical analysis and stability sensitivity analysis), and Month 8 (manuscript preparation).

items.title: A Hierarchical Negative Binomial Regression Analysis of Turbulence-Related Injury Counts in U.S. Part 121 Airline Operations
items.abstract: Turbulence remains one of the leading causes of in-flight injuries in commercial aviation, yet relatively little is known about the factors associated with differences in injury outcomes across turbulence encounter events. This study examined the environmental, operational, and human factors associated with turbulence-related injury counts in U.S. Part 121 operations using hierarchical negative binomial regression. A total of 184 turbulence-related injury events reported between 1995 and 2026 were analyzed, with predictor variables entered sequentially to evaluate the incremental contribution of each factor domain. Each retained predictor domain significantly improved model fit, and the final model achieved a Generalized R2 of 0.257. Wake turbulence category, phase of flight, and night duty emerged as significant predictors. Compared with large-category aircraft, heavy-category aircraft were associated with lower expected injury counts, whereas turbulence encountered during descent and during night duty was associated with higher expected injury counts. These findings suggest that turbulence-related injury outcomes are associated with environmental, operational, and human factors and provide empirical evidence to inform assessment of turbulence-related injury counts and future safety management strategies.

items.title: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework (HCAI-LAF) for Open and Distance Education
items.abstract: This chapter presents the Human Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework, a conceptual model designed to support valid, equitable, and trustworthy assessment in AI enhanced Open Distance e Learning environments. The chapter addresses challenges created by generative artificial intelligence in higher education, where submitted work may not fully represent learner understanding or skill. It integrates learner engagement, artifact authenticity, AI assessment support, instructor oversight, and transparency and trust into a unified sociotechnical framework centered on Learning Evidence Validity. The framework explains how human agency, ethical oversight, and artificial intelligence tools interact to influence the quality, reliability, and fairness of assessment outcomes. The chapter further outlines construct relationships and demonstrates how the framework can guide empirical research and practical implementation across online and hybrid contexts.

items.title: A Human–AI Orchestration Framework for Mathematics Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing personalized and adaptive education. Existing research has examined Human–AI hybrid adaptivity and coordination between human participants and AI systems, but clearer conceptualization is needed of the pedagogical coordination of functionally different forms of instructional support, particularly in highly abstract domains such as mathematics. This study proposes a Human–AI Orchestration Framework integrating Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs), Generative AI, and direct teacher support while retaining pedagogical orchestration and responsibility with the teacher. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, the Framework proposes Cognitive Load Redistribution as a theoretical proposition and introduces coordination mechanisms, including Handover Points and a Meta-Prompt. Its practical implementation was explored through an exploratory design pilot with 32 Grade 8 students in an authentic classroom, using observations and feedback to iteratively refine its configuration. The pilot informed several design refinements, including refinement of the Meta-Prompt, introduction of “Call the Teacher,” and adaptation of interaction formats. These formative observations provide preliminary indications of the practical feasibility of coordinating functionally different and potentially complementary forms of instructional support, while the Framework’s educational effectiveness and proposed conceptual mechanisms remain to be systematically evaluated in future research.

items.title: A hybrid artificial intelligence framework for three-dimensional electromagnetic field mapping using airborne measurements in general aviation
items.abstract: The increasing electrification of aircraft systems and development of autonomous aviation technologies increase the need for accurate characterization of electromagnetic field (EMF) distributions under operational conditions. However, dense three-dimensional EMF measurements in aviation environments are difficult to obtain because airborne observations are typically sparse, irregularly distributed, and collected under varying flight conditions. Here, we present an artificial intelligence-based framework for three-dimensional reconstruction of the electric field component of EMF from real-world airborne measurements in general aviation. The study uses more than 80 h of measurements collected during operational activities involving four aircraft types and a low-cost, high-sensitivity sensing platform recording synchronized electric-field and geospatial data over the 1-8000 MHz frequency range. Geostatistical and machine-learning approaches, including Kriging, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and Exact Gaussian Processes, were evaluated for three-dimensional field reconstruction. Based on this comparison, we developed a hybrid Deep Gaussian Process Kolmogorov-Arnold Feature Extractor (DGKAN), combining nonlinear feature representation with probabilistic spatial modeling and uncertainty estimation. DGKAN achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.0381 and a mean squared error of 0.0071, reducing the mean absolute error by approximately 27.6% relative to the strongest baseline model. These results demonstrate that combining Kolmogorov-Arnold representations with probabilistic Gaussian Process modeling enables accurate reconstruction of three-dimensional electromagnetic field distributions from sparse airborne measurements. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach for electromagnetic environment assessment in general aviation and establishes a basis for further development of intelligent EMF monitoring and prediction methods under operational flight conditions.

items.title: A multi-prompt transfer learning framework based on segment anything model 2 for segmenting microcracks in engineered cementitious composite images and videos
items.abstract: Accurate segmentation of engineered cementitious composites (ECC) microcracks is important for evaluating material damage and cracking behavior. However, ECC cracks are typically slender, low-contrast, and densely distributed, and can easily be confused with pores, shadows, and surface textures. Existing crack segmentation methods rely heavily on large-scale pixel-level annotations and often exhibit limited robustness when applied to ECC microcracks. To address these issues, this study proposes a multi-prompt transfer learning framework based on Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2). The framework integrates a threshold-based coarse-mask prior, a self-perceptive prompt box, and Euclidean distance transform-guided positive and negative point prompts to enhance crack localization while suppressing noise and preserving crack connectivity. In addition, a progressive unfreezing-based few-shot transfer strategy and a hybrid loss function are employed to effectively adapt the foundation model to the ECC crack domain while reducing annotation costs. Experimental results on a laboratory ECC dataset show that the proposed framework achieves a mean accuracy of 99.1%, a mean intersection over union (IoU) of 86.4%, and a Dice coefficient of 92.6%, outperforming mainstream deep learning baselines. Notably, with only five annotated training images, the framework still achieves a mean IoU of 81.7% and a Dice coefficient of 89.7%, demonstrating strong performance under a highly limited annotation budget. Without any video-specific training, the framework also achieves temporally consistent crack video segmentation through the streaming memory mechanism of SAM2. Overall, the proposed framework provides an effective and annotation-efficient method for detecting microcracks in both static images and dynamic videos.

items.title: A Multi-Stakeholder Survey Examining Incident Review Processes in a National Healthcare System: A Study Protocol
items.abstract: Background Incident reporting is central to patient safety, yet translating review findings into systemic learning remains challenging. Within the Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) 2020 Incident Management Framework (IMF), Improvement Planning and Monitoring (Step 6) is where findings are intended to become service change. How well reviews achieve this, and how the review methodologies in use shape that performance, has not been systematically examined. This protocol sets out a study examining how these methodologies operate in practice and the perceived quality of the recommendations they produce, by capturing the accounts of multiple stakeholders linked to the same reviews, with particular attention to human factors in the transition from learning to action. Methods The study uses a cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey design. A stratified random sample of 96 incident reviews will be drawn from the National Incident Management System (NIMS): 48 Category 1 (major/severe harm) and 48 Category 2 (moderate harm), equally divided between acute and community settings. Seven role-tailored instruments, mapped to four stakeholder categories (reviewers and commissioners; clinical staff; implementers; patients, service users and families), combine rating-scale and written-response questions organised around the six IMF principles. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive and non-parametric methods, qualitative data using reflexive thematic analysis, and the two strands integrated through joint displays. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been granted by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Trinity College Dublin and the HSE National Research Ethics Committee. A pilot phase of five reviews will precede national administration. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentation, and a summary report to the HSE, and are intended to identify systemic barriers to improvement planning and inform a national logic model for shared learning.

items.title: A New Frontier in the Digital Divide? Toward a Nuanced Understanding of Internet Unadopters
items.abstract: Conventionally, digital divide research focuses on people who have never used the internet (nonadopters). However, those who formerly adopted the internet but no longer use it (unadopters) are often neglected. Analysis of the 2016 and 2018 waves of the China Family Panel Studies reveals that the likelihood of internet unadoption in China increases with advancing age, decreasing income, and lower educational attainment. Those who are disadvantaged at the adoption stage are less likely to remain online later. In addition, the device divide is positively related to persistent internet use. Moreover, behavioral habitual use mediates the influence of perceived importance on internet unadoption and becomes a substantively important predictor of internet unadoption behavior. These findings validate the relevance of conventional user-focused digital divide initiatives, originally designed for nonadopters, in addressing the challenge of unadoption.

items.title: A paradigm shift toward explainable and federated intelligence for brain tumor MRI analysis
items.abstract: Deep learning techniques in brain tumor analysis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans have improved significantly, but their clinical deployment is limited by models with limited interpretability (‘black-box' models) and data privacy limitations. This paper analyses recent literature and aims to explore the intersection of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Federated Learning (FL). Following the PRISMA protocol, a systematic search was conducted in Scopus on February 24, 2026, covering English-language journal articles and conference proceedings published from January 2020 to February 2026. The search initially identified 767 records, which were screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria for MRI-based brain tumor studies addressing deep learning, explainability, privacy, or Federated Learning, resulting in 147 initially retained studies for the final screening set. One study was subsequently identified as formally retracted and excluded from the final synthesis, resulting in 146 included studies. The review classifies the literature into five primary research themes in brain tumor analysis: explainability, deep learning frameworks, privacy-preserving learning, advanced architectures (Transformers and Mamba), and multimodal learning. The literature suggests a paradigm shift in brain tumor analysis toward model interpretability using XAI. However, there is a significant knowledge gap in privacy-preserving collaborative learning models. Advanced architectures are proposed to solve brain tumor problems, but there are still limitations in model generalization, computational costs, and clinical reliability.

items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation
items.abstract: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.

items.title: A psychological prediction automatic reasoning framework for explaining potential cognitive states
items.abstract: Psychological prediction, the ability to infer human behavior and intentions, is essential for artificial intelligence and human–machine interaction. Existing deep learning models often rely on surface-level fitting and lack structured abductive interpretability, while traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from non-differentiable discontinuities and limited adaptability to dynamic contextual constraints. This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic automated reasoning framework for modeling latent cognitive states under contextual constraints. The framework introduces a context-aware adaptive SMC resampling operator (CAR-SMC), which uses energy-based penalties to filter hypotheses violating contextual constraints. We further design an executable differentiable program synthesis (EDPS) module and a hybrid iterative program–cognition interaction (HIPCI) mechanism. Through stop-gradient-based directional optimization, HIPCI separates the update pathways of belief and program representations during alternating fixed-point optimization, reducing circular gradient entanglement. Experiments on OpenToM and FANToM show that the framework improves the abductive consistency rate (ACR), an empirical belief–action consistency metric, to 70.8% and 52.1%, respectively. Under the adopted classification-oriented evaluation setup, these results indicate additional ACR gains over pure fine-tuned encoder classifiers and higher ACR than the evaluated few-shot ToT reference baseline (~ 7B), while using fewer parameters and maintaining an average inference latency of 215 ms per instance. Overall, this work provides a differentiable framework for machine Theory of Mind with process-level structural interpretability under the evaluated text-based classification setting.

items.title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets
items.abstract: Abstract The European Law Institute’s Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a right for consumers to use digital assistants in business-to-consumer relations. The DACC’s definition encompasses consumer AI agents (CAIAs), which use AI-generated outputs to determine transactionally relevant matters left open by consumers and initiate or perform transactional actions. The article examines two concerns. First, recognition and safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, causing consumers to overestimate CAIAs’ technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic markets, disproportionately benefit incumbents in adjacent digital markets, and foster concentration, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. Legislation should therefore first establish essential rules governing delegation, responsibility and market contestability. Technical implementation may be entrusted to European standardisation bodies, but the Commission’s request should define tasks precisely and maximise transparency and balanced stakeholder participation to mitigate legitimacy concerns. Only once CAIAs are sufficiently reliable and the legal framework more mature should the right to use a CAIA be recognised.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Analysis of AI-Driven Legacy System Modernization in the Public Sector
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper examines the socio-technical limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize legacy information systems in the public sector, where continuity of services, policy obligations, security, and public accountability shape technology decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The paper combines a review of literature on public-sector AI adoption and legacy-system modernization with an anonymous survey of more than 50 public-sector technology professionals. Participants represented technical, analytical, management, application-support, and project roles and a range of professional experience. Survey topics included AI benefits and risks, organizational readiness, security and privacy, governance, workforce challenges, and human oversight. Findings: Respondents recognized AI's potential to support modernization but raised concerns about citizen-data protection, compliance, trust in generated outputs, integration, workforce readiness, and accountability. The findings suggest that AI should augment, not replace, experienced professionals and established engineering controls. Survey responses also point to the importance of governance, training, secure environments, phased implementation, and human validation. Originality: The paper brings technical, organizational, institutional, and ethical constraints together in a public-sector legacy-modernization context. It emphasizes that AI should augment, rather than replace, accountable human expertise and that successful adoption depends on governance, secure data practices, validation, and organizational readiness. Research limitations/implications: The survey reflects the views of its participants and should not be treated as representative of all public-sector technology professionals. Environmental impacts were not directly measured in the structured survey. Further research could test these findings across agencies and modernization projects.

items.title: A sparse autoencoder and explainable machine learning framework for provenance tracing of historic blue bricks in architectural conservation
items.abstract: Provenance identification of historic blue bricks supports material authenticity in architectural conservation, but missing inscriptions and incomplete archives limit conventional approaches. We integrate sparse autoencoders, machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence to classify brick provenance using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence data. Spectral latent features are fused with elemental concentrations, and synthetic minority oversampling addresses class imbalance. In a dataset of 52 bricks from five regions, the random forest classifier achieved 95% test accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.973. Shapley additive explanations identified Rb, Al and Zr as important discriminative variables, while decoder-based analysis linked latent features to mineral phases. Ablation and feature-substitution analyses indicated complementary elemental and spectral information. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a high-accuracy and theoretically interpretable engineering solution for the provenance identification of historic blue bricks.

items.title: A Survey of Explainable Reinforcement Learning: Targets, Methods and Needs
items.abstract: The success of recent Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has been accompanied by the opacity of their internal mechanisms, due notably to the use of deep neural networks. In order to understand these internal mechanisms and explain the output of these AI models, a set of methods have been proposed, grouped under the domain of eXplainable AI (XAI). This paper focuses on a sub-domain of XAI, called eXplainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), which aims to explain the actions of an agent that has learned by reinforcement learning. We propose an intuitive taxonomy based on two questions ‘What’ and ‘How’. The first question focuses on the target that the method explains, while the second relates to the way the explanation is provided. We use this taxonomy to provide a state-of-the-art review of over 250 papers. In addition, we present a set of domains close to XRL, which we believe should get attention from the community. Finally, we identify some needs for the field of XRL.

items.abstract: Abstract Computational Thinking (CT) is increasingly expected across curricula, yet pre-service teachers often report limited preparation for translating CT concepts into instructional practice. This systematic literature review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) supports pre-service teachers’ instructional design and what the available evidence implies for CT-oriented teaching. Using the PRISMA approach, the review synthesised 26 empirical studies identified through Scopus and ScienceDirect under the original eligibility criteria. The evidence base was heterogeneous: only two studies were coded as explicitly addressing CT integration, fifteen as implicitly CT-aligned, and nine as having no identifiable CT integration. Accordingly, indirect studies are treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of CT instructional design. Across the literature, GenAI was used for ideation, lesson planning, feedback, multimedia generation, and iterative refinement. Several studies reported gains or positive experiences in efficiency, confidence, engagement, creativity, or instructional design competence; however, these outcomes were study-specific and should not be generalised as improvements in CT competence. Several studies have linked more productive use of GenAI to human evaluation, AI literacy, pedagogical or subject-matter knowledge, and structured frameworks or training. Reported risks included inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, hallucinations, overreliance, metacognitive laziness, and ethical concerns. Because the search was limited to Scopus and ScienceDirect and applied an open-access criterion, the review may be affected by database and accessibility bias. Overall, direct evidence that GenAI improves CT-specific instructional design remains preliminary; the broader literature more strongly supports a conditional role for GenAI as a pedagogical scaffold in CT-relevant instructional design.

items.title: A Topology-Guided GeoAI Agentic Framework for Urban Flood Screening
items.abstract: Open-world geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) agents can transform public geospatial data into accessible decision support for real-world challenges, but must balance autonomous reasoning with reliable spatial analysis and human oversight. We present a topology-guided GeoAI agentic framework for urban flood screening that takes a place name, drawn region, or uploaded boundary and returns ranked candidate basins with an interactive map and report. A deterministic controller retrieves public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure layers, extracts terrain depressions with discrete Morse theory, and ranks basins with a relative flood-priority score. The language model acts only at recorded decision points: selecting a persistence threshold from a precomputed candidate table, drafting recommendations from computed evidence, and reviewing each recommendation against the same evidence. Three human-in-the-loop checkpoints let users revise the threshold, factor weights, or recommendation. In a College Park, Maryland case study, the selected threshold reduced 278 raw terrain minima to 70 basins, with 77% of these basins' lowest points also identified as sinks by a separately computed eight-direction (D8) flow-routing model. Across four further study areas, agreement ranged from 61% to 83%. By combining open data, explicit spatial reasoning, traceable evidence, and human oversight, the framework enables transparent first-pass flood screening while keeping consequential recommendations inspectable and user-controlled.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Digital Life and Consciousness Engineering: From Tool-Oriented Agents to Evolving Digital Life
items.abstract: Contemporary agents built on large language models have approached the practical limits of generalpurpose task tools, yet commonly lack consistency, evolvability, purposefulness, and proactivity. These four deficiencies directly affect subjective user experience and long-term trust. Their underlying cause is not simply insufficient model scale or a missing standalone algorithm, but the absence of an overarching framework that closes the loop between a consistent self and self–world co-evolution. Existing consciousness theories address competing aspects of consciousness; cognitive architectures organize memory and metacognition without an endogenous self; and work on agent memory, planning, and self-improvement lacks a shared lifecycle. We propose a concise and operational unified framework organized around Four Selves—the Constitutional, Old (Autobiographical), New (Updated), and Ideal Selves—and Two Domains comprising an Inner World and an Outer World, the latter differentiated into Primordial, Old, New, and Perfect Worlds. Past, Present, and Future provide temporal coordinates; online and offline optimization form two evolutionary lanes; and perception, recording, monitoring, recollection, thinking, prediction, planning, and action constitute a closed cognitive loop. The proposed dynamics use self-discrepancy to motivate self-evolution and world-discrepancy to motivate environmental transformation, corresponding respectively to prediction-error-driven model updates and active-inference-driven action. All updates are projected onto an inviolable constitutional feasible set and committed only after validation. We formalize constrained updates and provide conditional guarantees for discrepancy descent and self–world allocation under explicit assumptions. A small two-backbone account-state evaluation demonstrates sensitivity to information organization, including cases where generic structured memory outperforms the Four-Self presentation, motivating more rigorous longitudinal tests. Here, consciousness engineering refers exclusively to constructing observable functions analogous to those associated with human consciousness; it does not imply subjective machine experience.

items.title: ABRA: Agent-Bound UI for Human-Agent Communication beyond Chat with Reusable Views
items.abstract: Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent-Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task-specific meanings. Agents bind task-specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework-agnostic prototype of Agent-Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM-backed agents on canvas authoring, owner-side consequence resolution, and cross-agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.

items.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses
items.abstract: AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.

items.title: Academic-year differences and psychophysiological associations with objective spinal parameters in physiotherapy students: a cross-sectional DIERS formetric 4D study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physiotherapy students are exposed to differing physical and psychological demands across classroom-based and clinical stages of training. Although musculoskeletal symptoms, stress, sleep quality and burnout have been widely investigated in healthcare students, these factors have rarely been examined together using objective three-dimensional spinal assessment. This study compared spinal parameters between third- and fourth-year physiotherapy students and examined their associations with academic-year-related physical exposure, psychophysiological factors, sleep quality, and physical activity. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 132 healthy physiotherapy students (70 third year and 62 fourth year) underwent three-dimensional spinal assessment using the DIERS Formetric 4D system. Trunk length, kyphotic angle and lordotic angle were recorded. Sleep quality, anxiety, burnout and physical activity were evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, Maslach Burnout Inventory and International Physical Activity Questionnaire. Group comparisons were performed, followed by hierarchical multiple linear regression analyses to examine independent associations and bootstrap mediation analyses to explore indirect associations. Multivariable analyses were adjusted for relevant anthropometric, academic-year, school-based standing and sitting, and physical activity variables. RESULTS: Fourth-year students reported longer school-based standing and shorter sitting durations than third-year students (both p < 0.001), alongside lower trait anxiety and burnout scores and higher walking activity. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in trunk length, kyphotic angle, or lordotic angle; kyphotic angle was numerically lower in fourth-year students but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.051). In the fully adjusted hierarchical model, trait anxiety (β = - 0.148, p = 0.022) and poorer sleep quality (PSQI; β = - 0.139, p = 0.032) were independently associated with shorter trunk length, whereas academic-year group and school-based standing and sitting durations were not. The final model explained 68.4% of trunk-length variance. Exploratory mediation analysis identified a significant indirect association between emotional exhaustion and trunk length through sleep quality (B = - 0.300, 95% bootstrap CI - 0.686 to - 0.062, p = 0.048), while the corresponding direct and total associations were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Objective spinal parameters did not differ significantly between third- and fourth-year physiotherapy students despite marked differences in their school-based standing and sitting exposure. Trunk length was independently associated with trait anxiety and sleep quality after multivariable adjustment, while exploratory analysis identified an indirect association between emotional exhaustion and trunk length through sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than temporal or causal relationships. Collectively, the results highlight the potential value of educational strategies that extend beyond ergonomic considerations to integrate biomechanical, psychological, and recovery-related factors during physiotherapy training. items.title: Accuracy and Efficiency of Articicial Intelligence Tools for Transcription in Qualitative Research
items.abstract: Verbatim transcription in qualitative research is hugely time consuming, yet critical for data validity. The rise in artificial intelligence tools for transcription provides new opportunities for researchers. We assessed the accuracy and efficiency of two widely accessible AI tools and human transcription to provide empirical guidance for researchers. We compared 10 verbatim transcripts generated via three transcription modes: human, Otter.ai and MAXQDA. We compared transcription time, cost, errors (volume and type), and correction time. Results show that the AI tools were highly time/cost efficient but had 2-3 times more errors than human transcription. Accounting for average correction time, AI tools generated a transcript in 1.25 - 2.5 hours for USD31-38 per transcript; thus 3–6 times faster and 3 times cheaper than human transcription. However, human review of AI transcription remains critical for data validity; thus, AI tools can assist in the transcription process versus generating the final product. We develop recommendations for each phase of the research process to maximize the benefits of using AI transcription tools.

items.title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
items.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

items.title: Adaptive Performance as a Pathway to Human Capital Readiness: The Roles of Digital Readiness and Organizational Resilience
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how learning agility and change self-efficacy are associated with human capital readiness through adaptive performance and whether digital readiness and organizational resilience condition these relationships. Using a quantitative explanatory design, cross-sectional survey data from 350 professional workers across government, state-owned enterprises, banking, higher education, and digital-based private organizations in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, were analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Learning agility (β = 0.186, p = 0.004) and change self-efficacy (β = 0.301, p < 0.001) were positively associated with adaptive performance, while adaptive performance was positively associated with human capital readiness (β = 0.498, p < 0.001). The model explained 74.6% of the variance in adaptive performance and 73.4% in human capital readiness. Digital readiness did not significantly moderate either capability-performance relationship. Organizational resilience strengthened the learning agility-adaptive performance relationship (β = 0.135, p = 0.010) but weakened the change self-efficacy-adaptive performance relationship (β = -0.196, p = 0.016). These findings position adaptive performance as a central behavioral pathway through which individual capabilities relate to workforce readiness and show that organizational context operates asymmetrically rather than uniformly. Organizations should pair digital investment with learning-oriented work design, confidence-building support, managerial flexibility, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms. items.title: Adoption and Impacts of a Socratic Generative AI Tutor in Undergraduate Algebra
items.abstract: Instructors looking to support personalized mathematics learning may provide access to generative AI tutoring tools. Few studies explore the effectiveness of these systems in classroom settings. This is particularly important in mathematics, where genAI is a shift from historic adaptive intelligent tutoring systems. We evaluated undergraduate algebra students’ (n=58) use of the Socratic generative AI tutor, Khanmigo, through a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study using survey, registrar, grades, and software usage data. One course section was assigned four Khanmigo activities throughout the semester (experimental), while the other was provided access and an introductory activity only (control). A Wilcoxon Rank Sum test showed that experimental students engaged in significantly more chats than control students (p<0.05), controlling for in-class activities. Instrumental help seeking was positively correlated with Khanmigo use, while intentions of seeking help from technology sources were negatively correlated with use. Khanmigo use did significantly predict mathematics grades after controlling for prior GPA and course section. Most students reported using Khanmigo for homework help and exam prep, though lack of visuals and the Socratic design limited perceived usefulness for some students. Integrating genAI tutoring systems into class activities and setting student expectations may improve the likelihood of students using them effectively for learning.

items.title: Advanced Product and Systems Design Engineering in the Era of Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT)
items.abstract: The rapid convergence of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), distributed sensor networks, and edge-native artificial intelligence has transformed modern technology from isolated mechanical devices into complex, interconnected ecosystems. At the heart of this transformation lies Product and Systems Design Engineering (PSDE), a multidisciplinary discipline that bridges mechatronic engineering, human-centered design, software architecture, and systems engineering. This paper presents an extended theoretical and methodological framework for PSDE tailored specifically to Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT)—collectively conceptualized as the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT).We systematically examine the multi-layered lifecycle of IoRT development, addressing critical trade-offs between dynamic mechanical optimization, deterministic edge-computing, wireless network latency, cyber-physical security, and human-robot interaction (HRI). Furthermore, we detail the implementation of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation paradigms as mechanisms for risk mitigation and cost reduction. The paper concludes by outlining future design directions under the Industry 5.0 paradigm, highlighting the role of generative design, bio-inspired robotics, and circular lifecycle economics.

items.title: Advancing Patient‐Centred AI With Adaptive Machine Learning
items.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

items.title: After the no: what a user does next when an AI declines (Study 1, with correction)
items.abstract: An observational study of what a user does on the next turn after a ChatGPT-style assistant declines, using WildChat-1M. The dependent variable (press / follow the offered route / reframe / disengage) has real variance. The preregistered predictors mostly do not. This record includes a retraction. An exploratory contrast (capability limits produce fewer re-asks than policy refusals; 10/17 vs 11/42, Fisher p=.024) was found to be a coding collision: "press" had absorbed "walk the route the assistant offered." Re-coded, it is 6/17 vs 10/42, p=.52. Retracted 2026-10-22. Two preregistered tests failed: H1' is under-identified (predictors near-constant and co-occurring) and H2 is untestable (no frustration markers in 42 boundary turns). The boundary classification was independently validated on 84 turns by a second blind coder: kappa=.952. The dependent-variable coding was single-coder, which is the limitation that produced the error. Files: the preregistration text published before data collection (with its sha256), the full results document including codebook, reliability, re-code and limitations, and a deposit note stating the exact status of each claim. No raw corpus text is redistributed.

items.title: AgentDP: Towards Automated Model Deployment for Heterogeneous Embedded AI Applications
items.abstract: This paper presents AgentDP, which aims to deploy pre-trained AI models on heterogeneous embedded devices by fully automating model optimization and adaptation (O&A) with Large Language Model (LLM) agents. AgentDP not only significantly reduces human effort via automation but also enhances model inference efficacy by integrating LLMs with device-specific domain knowledge. To deliver a robust automation framework, AgentDP develops novel solutions to address three key technical challenges: 1) To help users elicit clear requirements, we propose a user requirement standardization module; 2) To mitigate the execution environment mismatch between AI models and heterogeneous embedded devices, we design an operator-aware model partition paradigm that enables different parts of the model to be efficiently executed on distinct inference engines. 3) To avoid re-searching optimization hyperparameters for new tasks, we propose a configuration reuse module that heuristically retrieves previous hyperparameter configurations for efficient reuse. Extensive experiments demonstrate that by fully automating the entire O&A process, AgentDP reduces entire model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual O&A while achieving higher task accuracy (more than 13% on average) than the baselines. Additionally, a comprehensive user study also exhibits the robust generalizability of AgentDP in adapting to different user requirements for heterogeneous embedded devices.

items.title: Agentic AI-Driven Digital Twin Frameworks for Predictive Toxicology and Autonomous Drug Safety Assessment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and computational pharmacology are changing the current approach to modern predictive toxicology and drug safety assessment. Traditional toxicity assessment tools are based on animal testing and non-dynamic computational models which are frequently limited in terms of scalability, and real-time toxicity forecasting. In this chapter, an agentic AI-based digital twin platform of predictive toxicology and autonomous drug safety evaluation is introduced. The suggested framework combines multimodal biomedical analytics, explainable AI (XAI), graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and federated learning to represent an intelligent ecosystem of toxicology. The system aids the adaptive simulation of toxicity, predicting toxicity individually, real-time pharmacological monitoring, and pharmacovigilance based on AI, enhances interpretability and privacy-preserving biomedical intelligence. Other significant applications, regulatory issues and future perspectives of next-generation intelligent drug safety systems are also discussed.

items.title: Agentic AI-Powered Expiry Date Management System
items.abstract: Food and medicines that pass their expiry dates cause avoidable financial loss, health risk and environmental harm, yet most expiry-tracking tools are passive reminder lists that depend on manual data entry. This paper proposes an Agentic AIPowered Expiry Date Management System in which a team of cooperating, tool-using AI agents autonomously captures product labels, extracts and validates expiry dates with optical character recognition (OCR), estimates shelf life when no date is printed, ranks items by spoilage risk, and acts on the result by sending timely alerts, suggesting recipes and routing surplus items to donation partners. A central orchestrator agent plans tasks, calls specialised agents and learns from user feedback, while a shared knowledge layer keeps inventory and food-safety rules consistent. We describe the architecture, the riskscoring model and the agent workflow, and report an illustrative simulation of 500 households over 60 days in which the agentic prioritisation policy reduced wasted items from 21.5% to 14.8% (c = 0.7) and 13.3% (c = 0.9). The modular design allows each agent to be upgraded or deployed independently in households, retail shelves and hospital pharmacies.
